subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Framing Effect
description: A quick, practical guide to The Framing Effect.

hook.text: Would you prefer beef that is 75% lean or 25% fat? Same beef. Different frame. Different choice.

buildup.text: The framing effect: the way a choice is worded changes the decision—even when the options are identical.

discovery.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed that people choose surgery framed as "90% survival" over "10% mortality."

twist.text: Loss frames trigger risk-seeking. Gain frames trigger risk-aversion. The frame flips your strategy.

climax.text: Politicians, marketers, and lawyers engineer frames deliberately. The question is never neutral.

punchline.text: How you ask changes what they answer.

quiz.question: How does framing change decisions?
options: It changes how options are perceived without changing facts

details.summary: How information is presented, or framed, dramatically changes decisions even when the underlying facts are identical. Describing a surgery as having a 90 percent survival rate versus a 10 percent death rate produces different choices despite being logically equivalent.
details.whyItMatters: Framing effects show that humans are not purely rational decision-makers. They have enormous implications for medical communication, policy design, and marketing.
takeaways: Identical information framed differently produces different choices
Gain frames promote risk aversion; loss frames promote risk seeking
Tversky and Kahneman demonstrated framing with the Asian disease problem

faq.question: What is the Asian disease problem?
faq.answer: Tversky and Kahneman presented a scenario where 600 people face a deadly disease. When framed as saving 200 people, subjects chose the sure option. When framed as 400 dying, they chose the risky gamble. Same outcome, different frame, different choice.

faq.question: How can you protect yourself against framing effects?
faq.answer: Reframe the problem in multiple ways before deciding. Convert gain frames to loss frames and vice versa. Focus on absolute numbers rather than percentages. Ask whether your preference changes with different wordings; if it does, the frame is driving your choice.
